description: Kiaklo is the Zuni rain-priest hero who, sent by the kachina priest Ka'wimosa, journeyed to find the Middle Place (itiwana) where the Zuni would settle. According to Zuñi origin myth, Duck carried him to the council hall of the gods, where he learned the story of creation and the sacred dances; his quest brought the kachina ceremonies to the people.
source: Ruth Bunzel, 'Zuñi Origin Myths' (1932); native-languages.org Zuni Legends; Zuni oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Kiaklo (Kiaklu/Käklo) is a genuine Zuni figure whose 'talk' in the origin myth recounts the tribe's creation, the origin of his ceremony and the search for the middle. Input's note that Duck brought him to the council hall of the gods is accurate (Bunzel). His role links the kachina priesthood to the founding of Zuni ceremonialism.

description: The Koyemshi, or Mudhead clowns, are the sacred clowns of the Zuni. Their origin myth tells of a father who fathered nine children with his sister and, in remorse, rolled in the mud until his head was covered in bulbous welts; his children were born with the same knobs. Barred from dancing as kachinas, they serve as spokesmen and chorus, opening the Shalako ceremony with comic satire.
source: Tony Hillerman Portal (Koyemshi); Indiana University ScholarWorks, 'Origin of the Koyemshi'; native-languages.org Zuni Legends
research_notes: Attested and richly documented. The origin legend (incestuous father who rolled in mud, producing children born covered with bulbous welts) matches the Zuni accounts. They are barred from dancing as full kachinas and act as spokespersons, chorus, and satirists; roles include curer, director, warrior, messenger and sage. The input's 'fertility and laughter' framing is a fair gloss but the mud-welt origin is the core.

description: Ko'komiki'somm, also known as Komorkis, is the Moon in Blackfoot tradition, one of the eldest of the sacred Sky People (Sspommitapiiksi). Wife of the Sun, Naato'si, and mother of the stars, she is the serene ruler of the night whose most important child is the Morning Star, Iipisowaahs; she is also the grandmother of the hero Star-Boy, and watches over lovers and those who travel after dark.
source: native-languages.org Blackfoot Legends; Clark Wissler & D.C. Duvall, 'Mythology of the Blackfoot Indians' (1908)
research_notes: Attested. Ko'komiki'somma/Komorkis is the Blackfoot moon goddess, wife of Naato'si the Sun, mother of the star children; Morning Star (Iipisowaahs) is the most important of them and father of the mortal hero Star-Boy. Input's description (silver hair, robe of stars) is literary embellishment; the real substance is her role in the Sky World family. Culture field was 'USA' but should be Blackfoot/Siksika.

description: Kanati is the First Man and great hunter of Cherokee tradition, husband of Selu, the Corn Mother. His name derives from the Cherokee word for 'hunter' (often mistranslated as 'Lucky Hunter'). In the origin story he kept deer and game shut away in a cave and released them into the world, and once his wild son freed the animals, hunting became a necessity for humans.
source: native-languages.org Cherokee Legends; James Mooney, 'Myths of the Cherokee' (1900), sacred-texts.org
research_notes: Attested. Kanati is the Cherokee First Man and a guardian of the hunt; his name is from Kanohalidohi, 'hunter,' and 'Lucky Hunter' is a common mistranslation (native-languages.org). Mooney records his story at Pilot Knob: he released deer and other game from a cave, and after the Wild Boy freed them, men had to hunt. Husband of Selu (Corn), father of the culture hero.

description: Kashehotapalo, 'the woman caller,' is a being of Choctaw folklore that is neither man nor beast, with a small, shriveled old-man's head, a man's body, and the legs and cloven hooves of a deer. It dwells in low, swampy places and delights in creeping up behind hunters and crying out in a woman's voice to frighten them. It does not harm people, though it will warn game or enemies if it is angered.
source: Katherine Judson, 'Myths and Legends of the Mississippi Valley'; Wikipedia 'Choctaw mythology'; Access Genealogy
research_notes: Attested. Kashehotapalo is documented in Choctaw folklore (Judson; Wikipedia; Access Genealogy). The name literally means 'woman call' (kasheho=woman, tapalo=call). Details confirmed: small shriveled head, man's body, deer legs with cloven hooves, lives in low swamps, sneaks behind hunters and calls loudly in a woman's voice, delights in frightening but does not physically harm.

description: Kwanokasha is one of the Kowi Anukasha, the little people of Choctaw tradition, small cave-dwelling spirits beneath large rocks. He seizes boys who wander off and brings them before three ancient white-haired beings who offer a knife, herbs, and pebbles; the choice foretells a life as warrior, doctor, or one without power. He grants medicine gifts to the respectful but is dangerous to others.
source: native-languages.org Kowi Anukasha; Mike Boucher, Choctaw Legends; Choctaw oral tradition
research_notes: Attested. Kwanokasha belongs to the Kowi Anukasha ('forest dwellers'), the Choctaw Little People who live in caves under rocks (native-languages.org). The choice-of-knife/herbs/pebbles test matches the documented legend. He is a lesser being than the input's 'powerful spirit': dangerous only to disrespectful children, yet able to bestow medicine power. Analogues: Cherokee Tsvdigewi, Cree Mannegishi, Algonquian Pukwudgie.

description: Kolowa is a man-eating ogre of Creek (Muscogee) folklore, a huge, shaggy, humanlike creature covered in thick hair with enormous strength and a foul stench that can be smelled from far away. It lurks in the deep forests beyond the villages, imitates human voices to lure victims, and preys on people who stray too far from home; some modern storytellers liken it to a gorilla.
source: native-languages.org Creek Legends (Kolowa); Muscogee oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as a genuine Muscogee (Creek) figure, though documented mainly on native-languages.org and tribal tradition. Confirmed: huge, hairy, man-eating ogre of the deep forest with great strength, foul odor and a voice that imitates humans to lure prey. Some contemporary Creek storytellers translate 'Kolowa' as 'gorilla.' Related beings: Maneater of other Southeastern tribes, Double Face of the Plains.

description: Komokwa, 'Copper-Maker,' is the wealthy chief of the undersea world in Kwakwaka'wakw and Nuxalk tradition. He lives in a great copper house beneath the sea, its living posts the sea-lions, and rules the ocean's wealth. He tests heroes with dangerous trials, rewarding the worthy with copper, masks and songs; the winter counterpart of the sky Thunderbird, he guards his realm with an octopus.
source: Wikipedia 'Kwakwaka'wakw mythology' (Komokwa); Franz Boas, 'Kwakiutl Tales' (1910); Milwaukee Public Museum
research_notes: Attested. Komokwa/Kumugwe ('Copper-Maker,' 'wealthy one') is the undersea chief of the Kwakwaka'wakw and Nuxalk. Confirmed traits: house under the sea with living sea-lion posts, head so large it looks like an island, controls tides, eats human eyes like crab apples, guards the treasures of the sea (copper, blankets, coppers, songs, masks), keeps an octopus, and is identified with the winter ceremonial world opposite Thunderbird. Input's 'feathers/abalone headdress' is iconographic gloss; substance is accurate.

description: Kulus is the younger brother (or sister) of the Kwakwaka'wakw Thunderbird, Tseiqami, and a founding ancestor of many clans. Lacking the Thunderbird's spiral horns and lightning eyes, Kulus wears a coat of thick white down so warm that he sweats, sheds it, and becomes human. A Kulus who flew from the sky and removed his costume founded a clan; he helps raise ceremonial house beams.
source: U'mista Cultural Society, 'Living Tradition'; Wikipedia 'Kwakwaka'wakw mythology'; Franz Boas, 'Kwakiutl Tales' (1910)
research_notes: Attested. Kulus (Kolus) is the younger brother/sister of the Kwakwaka'wakw Thunderbird (Tseiqami), documented by the U'mista Cultural Society and Wikipedia. Key traits confirmed: no spiral horns, thick white down instead of feathers, overheats and sheds the covering to become human, flies down from heaven to become the founding ancestor of clans, helps humans raise big-house beams. The input's 'child of Thunderbird who survived an epic battle' is not the standard account.

A shape-shifter and thief of supernatural powers, he stole the sun, moon and stars from a stingy keeper, letting light into the world, and brought people fresh water and fire.

description: The Raven is a creator and culture hero of the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl). In the creation account, Raven (Kwekwaxa'we, 'Great-Inventor,' also U'melth) flew over the waters and made islands by dropping pebbles into the sea, then created the trees and grass and, after failed attempts, shaped the first man and woman from wood and clay; he brought the people the moon, fire, salmon and the tides.

research_notes: Attested. The input's 'guardian of caves' framing is invented; the genuine role is creator-culture hero.

description: The raven (gáagii, often not distinguished from the crow) is a genuine figure in Navajo tradition, closely linked with Coyote. In the Diné Bahane', the raven served as a spy for the monster birds, warning Changing Woman's twin sons to keep away, and the obsolescent Ravenway ceremony was connected with Coyoteway. Crows and ravens also figure in Navajo beliefs about skinwalkers and the dead.
source: Guy H. Cooper, 'Coyote in Navajo Religion and Cosmology' (1987); Zolbrod, 'Diné Bahane'; FeatherSnap, 'Crows and Ravens in Native Traditions'
research_notes: Attested as a genuine Navajo figure, though not as an 'animal-spirit guardian of forests.' The Navajo do not distinguish raven from crow (both gáagii); raven appears in the emergence story as a spy for the monsters (Zolbrod's Diné Bahane'), is linked with Coyote, and has an obsolescent Ravenway ceremonial tied to Coyoteway (Cooper 1987). Crows are also associated with skinwalkers. The guardian framing is invented.

The Blackfoot afterlife is the Sand Hills (spa'yi-ksiksin), where the souls of the dead reside; water beings are the Horned Snakes, not restless ravens or ghosts (native-languages.org; Wissler & Duvall 1908). The record is template filler ('phasing through objects, storm calling, energy manipulation'). Marked unattested.
